question: During which Five Year Plan of India was the slogan 'Garibi Hatao' given?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fifth Five Year Plan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The slogan "Garibi Hatao" (Remove Poverty) was associated with the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974-1979), launched under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. (गरीबी हटाओ — पाँचवीं पंचवर्षीय योजना)

 

• The twin objectives of the plan were "removal of poverty (Garibi Hatao)" and "attainment of self-reliance". It stressed employment generation, poverty alleviation and justice for the weaker sections.

 

• The Minimum Needs Programme (MNP) was introduced during this plan, along with the Twenty Point Programme (1975). The Indian National Highway System was also introduced in this period.

 

• The plan was terminated a year early, in 1978, by the Janata Government, which introduced a Rolling Plan for 1978-1980.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key Five Year Plans and their distinguishing features:
◦ First (1951-56) — based on the Harrod-Domar model; priority to agriculture and irrigation; the most successful plan.
◦ Second (1956-61) — based on the P.C. Mahalanobis model; priority to heavy industry; the Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956 belongs to this plan.
◦ Third (1961-66) — the Gadgil Yojana; aimed at a self-reliant economy, but failed because of two wars and a drought, leading to a Plan Holiday (1966-69).
◦ Fourth (1969-74) — growth with stability; nationalisation of 14 banks and the Green Revolution.
◦ Sixth (1980-85) — beginning of economic liberalisation; NABARD set up in 1982.
◦ Twelfth (2012-17) — the last Five Year Plan; theme of faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth.

 

• The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

 

NOTE

 

• Third Five Year Plan (Option 1): 1961-66, the Gadgil Yojana.

 

• Fourth Five Year Plan (Option 2): 1969-74, aiming at growth with stability.

 

• Sixth Five Year Plan (Option 4): 1980-85, which continued the anti-poverty programmes but is not associated with the slogan itself.

question: What is the literal meaning of the term 'Jina', from which the religion Jainism derives its name?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The conqueror.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word "Jina" literally means "the conqueror" — one who has conquered his senses, desires and passions. Those who follow the Jina are called Jainas, and the religion Jainism. (जिन — विजेता)

 

• The great teachers of Jainism are called Tirthankaras, meaning "ford-makers" — those who build a crossing over the ocean of worldly existence. There were 24 Tirthankaras, the first being Rishabhanatha (Adinatha) and the last Mahavira.

 

• Mahavira (599-527 BCE) was the 24th Tirthankara. Born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, his personal name was Vardhamana. He attained *kaivalya* (omniscience) at Jrimbhikagrama on the bank of the Rijupalika river, and was thereafter called Mahavira, Jina and Nirgrantha. He died at Pavapuri in Bihar.

 

• The 23rd Tirthankara, Parshvanatha, preached four vows; Mahavira added the fifth, Brahmacharya (celibacy). The Five Vows are Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Aparigraha and Brahmacharya, and the Three Jewels (Triratna) are Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jainism split into two sects — the Digambaras (sky-clad) and the Svetambaras (white-clad) — during the famine in Magadha in the time of Chandragupta Maurya.

 

• Jain councils: the First at Pataliputra under Sthulabhadra, and the Second at Valabhi under Devardhi Kshamasramana, where the 12 Angas were finally compiled.

 

NOTE

 

• The enlightened one (Option 1): This is the meaning of "Buddha", from the root *budh*, to awaken or to know.

 

• The liberated one (Option 3): Closer to the idea of "Siddha" or one who has attained *moksha*, but not the meaning of "Jina".

 

• The great teacher (Option 4): Corresponds to terms such as "Guru" or "Tirthankara", not to "Jina".

question: The ancient trade route known as the 'Uttarapatha' connected the Gangetic plains with which region?
option_1: The Deccan plateau up to Pratishthana
option_2: The north-western region up to Taxila
option_3: The eastern coast up to Tamralipti
option_4: The Malabar coast up to Muziris
solution_text:
The correct answer is The north-western region up to Taxila.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Uttarapatha, literally the "northern route", was the great ancient highway running from the Gangetic plains westward and north-westward up to Taxila and beyond into Central Asia. (उत्तरापथ — उत्तरी व्यापार मार्ग)

 

• It linked important cities such as Pataliputra, Kashi, Prayag, Kaushambi, Mathura, Hastinapura, Indraprastha and Taxila, and connected onwards with the Silk Route.

 

• Its southern counterpart was the Dakshinapatha, the "southern route", which ran from the Gangetic plains through Ujjain and Pratishthana (Paithan) to the ports of the western coast.

 

• The Mauryan emperor Ashoka maintained the route, planting shade trees, digging wells and building rest houses along it. In the medieval period Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and extended much of this alignment as the Sadak-e-Azam, later known as the Grand Trunk Road.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Taxila (Takshashila), in present-day Pakistan, was a renowned centre of learning where Chanakya is said to have taught, and it was the capital of the Gandhara Mahajanapada.

 

• Important ancient ports: Tamralipti (Bengal), Bharuch (Barygaza) and Sopara on the west coast, Arikamedu and Kaveripattinam (Puhar) in the south, and Muziris in Kerala. Many are described in the Greek text "The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea".

 

• India's principal exports in ancient times were spices, textiles, ivory and precious stones, and the chief import was gold, which led the Roman writer Pliny to complain that Rome was being drained of its wealth.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 describes the Dakshinapatha, the southern route, not the Uttarapatha.

 

• Option 3 describes the route to the eastern seaboard, of which Tamralipti was the chief port.

 

• Option 4 describes the maritime trade of the Malabar coast, associated with Roman commerce.

question: What is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system called?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Neuron.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The neuron, or nerve cell, is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It is the longest cell in the human body. (तंत्रिका कोशिका — तंत्रिका तंत्र की संरचनात्मक एवं क्रियात्मक इकाई)

 

• A neuron has three main parts:
◦ Cyton (cell body) — contains the nucleus and cytoplasm
◦ Dendrites — short branched projections that receive impulses
◦ Axon — a single long fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body

 

• The junction between two neurons is called a synapse, and the gap between an axon and a muscle is the neuromuscular junction. Impulses travel across a synapse by means of chemicals called neurotransmitters, such as acetylcholine and dopamine.

 

• The human nervous system is divided into the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord) and the Peripheral Nervous System, which includes the autonomic system with its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The brain has three main parts: the cerebrum (the largest part, seat of intelligence, memory and voluntary action), the cerebellum (balance and coordination) and the medulla oblongata (control of involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure). The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst.

 

• A reflex action is an automatic response that does not involve the brain; the pathway followed is the reflex arc, which passes through the spinal cord.

 

NOTE

 

• Nephron (Option 1): The structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney contains about 10 lakh (one million) nephrons.

 

• Axon (Option 3): A part of the neuron, not the unit itself.

 

• Alveolus (Option 4): The tiny air sac in the lungs where the exchange of gases takes place.

question: What is the maximum permissible gap between two consecutive sessions of the Indian Parliament?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Six months.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under Article 85(1) of the Constitution, the President shall summon each House of Parliament at such intervals that not more than six months shall intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. (अनुच्छेद 85 — दो सत्रों के बीच अधिकतम छह माह का अंतराल)

 

• In effect this means that Parliament must meet at least twice a year, though in practice it holds three sessions:
◦ Budget Session — February to May, the longest session
◦ Monsoon Session — July to August/September
◦ Winter Session — November to December, the shortest session

 

• The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum number of days of sitting.

 

• Related terms: Summoning (calling the House to meet), Adjournment (suspending work for a specified time), Adjournment sine die (terminating a sitting for an indefinite period), Prorogation (ending a session, done by the President) and Dissolution (ending the life of the Lok Sabha).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The quorum for a sitting of either House is one-tenth of the total membership (Article 100).

 

• The Lok Sabha has a maximum strength of 550 (530 from states, 20 from Union Territories); the Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250, of whom 12 are nominated by the President for their distinction in literature, science, art and social service.

 

• The first hour of every sitting is the Question Hour, and the period immediately after it is the Zero Hour, which is an Indian innovation and finds no mention in the Rules of Procedure.

 

NOTE

 

• Three months (Option 1), Four months (Option 2) and One year (Option 4) are incorrect. The figure of six months under Article 85 is the one tested in examinations, and it should not be confused with the three sessions ordinarily held in a year.

question: The Asiatic Society of Bengal, which pioneered the modern study of India's ancient past, was founded in 1784 by ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sir William Jones.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded at Calcutta in 1784 by Sir William Jones, a judge of the Supreme Court at Fort William, with the support of Governor-General Warren Hastings. (एशियाटिक सोसाइटी ऑफ बंगाल — विलियम जोन्स, 1784)

 

• Sir William Jones was a distinguished Orientalist who studied Sanskrit and in 1786 put forward the theory that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin had descended from a common ancestral language — the foundation of the Indo-European family of languages.

 

• He translated Kalidasa's "Abhijnanashakuntalam" into English in 1789 and also translated the Manusmriti. The Society's journal, Asiatick Researches, became the principal vehicle for the study of Indian antiquity.

 

• The Society was renamed the Asiatic Society in 1832, the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1832, and finally The Asiatic Society in 1951.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Orientalists, such as Jones and H.T. Colebrooke, admired Indian classical learning; the Anglicists, led by Lord Macaulay, held it in contempt. Macaulay's Minute on Education (1835) decided the controversy in favour of English education.

 

• The Archaeological Survey of India was established in 1861, with Alexander Cunningham as its first Director-General; he is called the Father of Indian Archaeology. John Marshall was the Director-General when the Indus Valley Civilisation was discovered in 1921-22.

 

NOTE

 

• James Mill (Option 1): Author of "The History of British India" (1817), in which he divided Indian history into the Hindu, Muslim and British periods — a periodisation long criticised for being based on religion.

 

• James Prinsep (Option 3): The scholar who deciphered the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts in 1837, making the Ashokan edicts readable.

 

• Alexander Cunningham (Option 4): The first Director-General of the ASI, who surveyed many ancient sites using the accounts of Hiuen Tsang.

question: 'Powada', a form of ballad narrating the heroic deeds of warriors, belongs to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Powada (Povada) is a traditional ballad form of Maharashtra, sung to narrate the heroic deeds of warriors, most often the exploits of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. (पोवाडा — महाराष्ट्र)

 

• The singers are called Shahirs, and the form is vigorous and declamatory rather than melodic, being intended to rouse the listener. The earliest known Powada, on the killing of Afzal Khan, was composed by the Shahir Agindas in the seventeenth century.

 

• During the freedom struggle the Powada was used to spread nationalist feeling, and it continued as a medium of social reform in the twentieth century.

 

• Other folk forms of Maharashtra: Lavani (a lively song-and-dance form accompanied by the *dholki*), Tamasha (folk theatre), Bharud, Gondhal, Koli dance and Dindi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ballad and narrative folk traditions of other states frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Pandavani — Chhattisgarh, narrating the Mahabharata; popularised by Teejan Bai
◦ Alha — Uttar Pradesh and Bundelkhand, on the heroes Alha and Udal
◦ Villu Paatu (bow song) — Tamil Nadu
◦ Burrakatha — Andhra Pradesh
◦ Baul — West Bengal, the songs of wandering mystics
◦ Pabuji ki Phad — Rajasthan, narrated before a painted scroll

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 2): Known for Garba, Dandiya Raas, Bhavai and Tippani.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Known for Ghoomar, Kalbelia, Mand singing and Khyal folk theatre.

 

• Karnataka (Option 4): Known for Yakshagana, Dollu Kunitha and Veeragase.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding friction?

I. Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.

II. Ball bearings are used in machines in order to reduce friction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (घर्षण — लोटनिक घर्षण सबसे कम; बॉल बेयरिंग से घर्षण में कमी)

 

• Statement I is correct: for the same pair of surfaces, rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which in turn is smaller than static friction. The order is therefore:
◦ Static friction > Sliding (kinetic) friction > Rolling friction
◦ This is precisely why wheels were among the most important of human inventions, and why heavy luggage is fitted with rollers.

 

• Statement II is correct: ball bearings are placed between moving parts of machinery so that sliding friction is replaced by rolling friction, thereby greatly reducing friction and wear. They are used in ceiling fans, bicycles, motor vehicles and machine shafts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Friction is the force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It arises from the interlocking of irregularities on the two surfaces.

 

• Disadvantages of friction: it causes wear and tear of machine parts, produces heat and wastes energy.

 

• Advantages of friction: it enables us to walk, allows vehicles to move and stop, permits writing with a pen and the striking of a matchstick, and prevents objects from slipping. Friction is therefore often called a "necessary evil".

 

• Methods of reducing friction: using lubricants (oil and grease), ball bearings, polishing surfaces, and streamlining the shape of vehicles, aircraft and ships to reduce fluid friction (drag).

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: Which Indian language was the first to be accorded the status of a classical language, in the year 2004?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tamil.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tamil was the first Indian language to be declared a classical language, in 2004. (तमिल — प्रथम शास्त्रीय भाषा, 2004)

 

• The languages subsequently granted classical status are:
◦ Sanskrit — 2005
◦ Telugu and Kannada — 2008
◦ Malayalam — 2013
◦ Odia — 2014
◦ Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali — 2024

 

• With these additions the total number of classical languages is eleven.

 

• The criteria for classical status include a recorded history of 1,500 to 2,000 years, a body of ancient literature regarded as a valuable heritage, an original literary tradition not borrowed from another speech community, and a distinction between the classical language and its modern form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution contains 22 languages. It began with 14; Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967), Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali by the 71st Amendment (1992), and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003).

 

• Article 343 declares Hindi in the Devanagari script to be the official language of the Union; India has no national language.

 

• Classical status brings benefits such as international awards for scholars, a Centre of Excellence for Studies in the language, and university chairs.

 

NOTE

 

• Sanskrit (Option 1): Declared a classical language in 2005, the year after Tamil.

 

• Telugu (Option 3) and Kannada (Option 4): Both declared classical languages in 2008.

question: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between the Indian National Congress and which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Muslim League.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between the Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League, concluded at their sessions held simultaneously at Lucknow. (लखनऊ समझौता — कांग्रेस एवं मुस्लिम लीग, 1916)

 

• Its two great achievements were:
◦ The reunion of the Moderates and the Extremists within the Congress, who had split at the Surat Session of 1907. The Lucknow session was presided over by Ambica Charan Mazumdar.
◦ Congress-League unity, with the Congress accepting the Muslim League's demand for separate electorates, and both bodies jointly demanding self-government for India.

 

• Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah were the principal architects of the pact; Jinnah was then described as the "Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity" by Sarojini Naidu.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important agreements of the freedom struggle:
◦ Poona Pact (1932) — between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, replacing separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats within the general electorate. It followed the Communal Award of Ramsay MacDonald.
◦ Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) — suspending the Civil Disobedience Movement; Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference.
◦ Delhi Pact / Desai-Liaqat Pact (1945).

 

• The Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906 by Nawab Salimullah and Aga Khan. Separate electorates had been introduced by the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms).

 

NOTE

 

• The Hindu Mahasabha (Option 2): Founded in 1915; it was not a party to the pact.

 

• The British Government (Option 3): The pact was an agreement between two Indian organisations; their joint demands were then placed before the British.

 

• The Swaraj Party (Option 4): Founded much later, in 1923, by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.

question: In the context of school education in India, what does the acronym 'NIPUN' in the NIPUN Bharat Mission stand for?
option_1: National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy
option_2: National Institute for Primary and Upper-primary Nurturing
option_3: New Integrated Plan for Universal Nutrition
option_4: National Improvement Programme for Under-privileged Nurseries
solution_text:
The correct answer is National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• NIPUN stands for National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy. (निपुण भारत मिशन)

 

• The NIPUN Bharat Mission was launched by the Ministry of Education in July 2021 under the aegis of the Samagra Shiksha scheme, in pursuance of the National Education Policy, 2020.

 

• Its goal is to ensure that every child attains foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) by the end of Grade 3, that is, the ability to read with understanding and to perform basic mathematical operations. The target year is 2026-27.

 

• The mission covers children in the age group of 3 to 9 years, and works through a five-tier implementation mechanism at the national, state, district, block and school levels.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word "Nipun" in Hindi itself means skilled or proficient, which makes the acronym especially apt.

 

• Related education initiatives: Samagra Shiksha, PM SHRI Schools, PM POSHAN (the renamed Mid-Day Meal scheme), DIKSHA (the digital learning platform), Vidya Pravesh (a school preparation module for Grade 1) and the National Curriculum Framework for Foundational Stage (2022).

 

• The National Education Policy 2020, which replaced the policy of 1986, introduced the 5+3+3+4 school structure in place of 10+2, and was framed by a committee headed by Dr. K. Kasturirangan.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 2, 3 and 4 are invented expansions. None of them corresponds to any scheme of the Government of India; each has been constructed by fitting plausible words to the letters of the acronym.

question: The rate of change of velocity of an object with respect to time is known as ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is acceleration.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity with time. (त्वरण — वेग परिवर्तन की दर)
◦ a = (v − u) / t, where u is the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time taken.
◦ Its SI unit is m/s², and it is a vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction.

 

• If the velocity decreases with time, the acceleration is negative and is called retardation or deceleration.

 

• Related definitions frequently tested together:
◦ Speed — the rate of change of distance; a scalar; SI unit m/s.
◦ Velocity — the rate of change of displacement; a vector; SI unit m/s.
◦ Distance — the total path length covered; a scalar.
◦ Displacement — the shortest distance between the initial and final positions; a vector.
◦ Momentum — the product of mass and velocity (p = mv); a vector; SI unit kg m/s.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three equations of motion for uniform acceleration:
◦ v = u + at
◦ s = ut + ½at²
◦ v² = u² + 2as

 

• Newton's Second Law states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, giving F = ma. The SI unit of force is the newton (N), where 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

 

• In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes continuously, so the body is accelerated; this centripetal acceleration is directed towards the centre.

 

NOTE

 

• Speed (Option 1): The distance travelled in unit time — a scalar quantity that says nothing about direction.

 

• Momentum (Option 2): The product of mass and velocity, not the rate of change of velocity.

 

• Displacement (Option 4): The shortest distance between two points, measured in metres, not a rate at all.

question: What is a 'deepfake', a term frequently in the news in recent years?
option_1: A method of encrypting data stored deep within a server
option_2: Synthetic audio or video in which a person's likeness or voice is convincingly replaced using artificial intelligence
option_3: A technique for recovering permanently deleted computer files
option_4: A form of undersea optical fibre cable used for internet traffic
solution_text:
The correct answer is Synthetic audio or video in which a person's likeness or voice is convincingly replaced using artificial intelligence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A deepfake is synthetic media — an image, audio clip or video — in which a person's face or voice is replaced by that of another so convincingly that the result appears genuine. (डीपफेक — कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता द्वारा निर्मित नकली सामग्री)

 

• The word is a combination of "deep learning" and "fake". The technology relies on a form of machine learning called a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), in which two neural networks — a generator and a discriminator — work against each other until the forgery becomes difficult to detect.

 

• The dangers include misinformation and election manipulation, financial fraud, defamation, identity theft and the erosion of public trust in genuine recordings.

 

• In India, such content is dealt with under the Information Technology Act, 2000, the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita relating to cheating by impersonation and forgery. Advisories have been issued to social media intermediaries requiring the labelling of synthetically generated content.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related terms often asked together: Phishing (fraudulent messages designed to steal credentials), Vishing (the same by voice call), Ransomware (malware that encrypts data for a ransom), GPS spoofing (transmitting false satellite signals to mislead navigation) and Cyberstalking.

 

• India's cybercrime reporting portal is cybercrime.gov.in, and the national helpline number is 1930. The nodal agency for cyber security incidents is CERT-In.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 describes encryption, which protects data rather than falsifies it.

 

• Option 3 describes data recovery or digital forensics.

 

• Option 4 describes submarine communication cables, which are a matter of physical infrastructure.

question: Under the flexible inflation targeting framework, the medium-term inflation target set for the Reserve Bank of India is ______.
option_1: 2 per cent with a band of +/- 2 per cent
option_2: 4 per cent with a band of +/- 2 per cent
option_3: 5 per cent with a band of +/- 2 per cent
option_4: 6 per cent with a band of +/- 2 per cent
solution_text:
The correct answer is 4 per cent with a band of +/- 2 per cent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework, the Government of India, in consultation with the RBI, has fixed the inflation target at 4 per cent, with an upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent and a lower tolerance limit of 2 per cent. (मुद्रास्फीति लक्ष्य — 4% (+/- 2%))

 

• The target is measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) — Combined, compiled by the National Statistical Office.

 

• The framework was adopted following the recommendations of the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and was given statutory force by the amendment of the RBI Act, 1934 through the Finance Act, 2016. The target is notified for a period of five years at a time.

 

• The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is responsible for fixing the policy repo rate to achieve the target. It has six members — three from the RBI, including the Governor as its ex-officio Chairperson, and three appointed by the Government. Decisions are taken by majority, and the Governor has a casting vote in the event of a tie. The MPC ordinarily meets six times a year.

 

• If the average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI is deemed to have failed and must report to the Government explaining the reasons and the remedial action proposed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key rates to remember: the repo rate (at which the RBI lends to commercial banks), the reverse repo rate, the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), the Bank Rate, the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

 

• Wholesale Price Index (WPI) inflation is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, while CPI is compiled by the NSO under MoSPI.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 3 and 4 are incorrect. The figure to remember is 4 per cent, with a tolerance band of two percentage points on either side, giving a range of 2 to 6 per cent.

question: The novel 'Train to Pakistan', set against the background of the Partition of India, was written by ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khushwant Singh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Train to Pakistan" (1956) was written by Khushwant Singh. (ट्रेन टू पाकिस्तान — खुशवंत सिंह)

 

• The novel is set in the fictional border village of Mano Majra in the summer of 1947, and describes how a community in which Sikhs and Muslims had lived peaceably together is torn apart by the violence of Partition. It won the Grove Press India Fiction Prize.

 

• Khushwant Singh's other well-known works: "I Shall Not Hear the Nightingale", "Delhi: A Novel", "The Company of Women", "A History of the Sikhs" and his autobiography "Truth, Love and a Little Malice".

 

• He edited *The Illustrated Weekly of India* and *The Hindustan Times*, was a member of the Rajya Sabha, and was awarded the Padma Bhushan (1974), which he returned in 1984 in protest against Operation Blue Star, and later the Padma Vibhushan (2007).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important works on the Partition:
◦ "Tamas" — Bhisham Sahni, which won the Sahitya Akademi Award
◦ "A Bend in the Ganges" — Manohar Malgonkar
◦ "Azadi" — Chaman Nahal, Sahitya Akademi Award winner
◦ "Ice-Candy Man" (Cracking India) — Bapsi Sidhwa
◦ "Toba Tek Singh" — Saadat Hasan Manto, a celebrated short story
◦ "Midnight's Children" — Salman Rushdie, Booker Prize 1981

 

NOTE

 

• Bhisham Sahni (Option 2): Author of "Tamas", also on the Partition, and a noted Hindi writer.

 

• Manohar Malgonkar (Option 3): Author of "A Bend in the Ganges" and "The Devil's Wind".

 

• Chaman Nahal (Option 4): Author of "Azadi", another major Partition novel.

question: Who is the author of the book 'The Turbulent Years: 1980-1996'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pranab Mukherjee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Turbulent Years: 1980-1996" was written by Pranab Mukherjee, the 13th President of India (2012-2017). (द टर्बुलेंट इयर्स — प्रणब मुखर्जी)

 

• It is the second volume of his memoirs, which form a trilogy:
◦ "The Dramatic Decade: The Indira Gandhi Years" — covering 1969 to 1980
◦ "The Turbulent Years: 1980-1996"
◦ "The Coalition Years: 1996-2012"

 

• Pranab Mukherjee held almost every senior portfolio in the Union Cabinet — Finance, Defence, External Affairs and Commerce — and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2019.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Memoirs and biographies by Indian public figures frequently asked in SSC:
◦ "My Country My Life" — L.K. Advani
◦ "Backstage: The Story Behind India's High Growth Years" — Montek Singh Ahluwalia
◦ "India Wins Freedom" — Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
◦ "Waiting for a Visa" — Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
◦ "Matoshree" and "Playing to Win" — Saina Nehwal
◦ "The Accidental Prime Minister" — Sanjaya Baru, on Manmohan Singh's first term
◦ "Straight Talk" — Yashwant Sinha

 

NOTE

 

• Manmohan Singh (Option 2): The former Prime Minister did not write a memoir of this title; the well-known account of his tenure, *The Accidental Prime Minister*, was written by his media adviser Sanjaya Baru.

 

• L.K. Advani (Option 3): Author of the autobiography "My Country My Life" (2008).

 

• Arun Jaitley (Option 4): A former Finance Minister and a prolific writer of columns, but not the author of this book.

question: The establishment of NABARD in 1982 was recommended by which of the following committees?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shivaraman Committee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The establishment of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was recommended by the Shivaraman Committee, formally the Committee to Review Arrangements for Institutional Credit for Agriculture and Rural Development (CRAFICARD). (शिवरामन समिति — नाबार्ड की स्थापना)

 

• The committee was set up by the Reserve Bank of India on 30 March 1979 under the chairmanship of Shri B. Sivaraman, a former member of the Planning Commission.

 

• NABARD was established on 12 July 1982 under an Act of Parliament (Act 61 of 1981), with its headquarters at Mumbai. It is the apex development bank for agriculture and rural development in India.

 

• Its functions include refinancing rural credit institutions such as Regional Rural Banks, State Cooperative Banks and District Central Cooperative Banks, promoting the Self Help Group-Bank Linkage Programme, administering the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), and supervising cooperative banks and RRBs.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important committees in Indian banking:
◦ Narasimham Committee I (1991) and II (1998) — banking sector reforms
◦ Malhotra Committee (1993) — insurance sector reforms, leading to the IRDA
◦ Khusro Committee (1989) — agricultural credit review
◦ Vaghul Committee — money market reforms
◦ Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) — comprehensive financial services for small businesses and low-income households, which led to Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks
◦ Rangarajan Committee — financial inclusion, and later poverty estimation

 

NOTE

 

• Narasimham Committee (Option 2): Concerned with the reform of the banking sector as a whole, not with the creation of NABARD.

 

• Khusro Committee (Option 3): The Agricultural Credit Review Committee (1989), which examined the working of the rural credit system after NABARD had already been established.

 

• Vaghul Committee (Option 4): Associated with the development of the money market in India.

question: The terms 'tee', 'birdie' and 'bogey' are associated with which of the following sports?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Golf.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tee, birdie and bogey are all terms used in golf. (गोल्फ)
◦ Tee — the small peg on which the ball is placed at the start of a hole, and also the area from which the first stroke is played.
◦ Par — the standard number of strokes a good player should need to complete a hole.
◦ Birdie — completing a hole in one stroke under par.
◦ Eagle — two strokes under par; Albatross — three under par.
◦ Bogey — one stroke over par; Double bogey — two over par.
◦ Hole in one (Ace) — sinking the ball with a single stroke from the tee.

 

• Other golf terms: caddie (the person who carries the clubs), fairway, green, bunker, putt, links and stroke play.

 

• A standard golf course has 18 holes. The four Major championships are the Masters Tournament, the PGA Championship, the US Open and The Open Championship (British Open).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Notable Indian golfers: Jeev Milkha Singh, Anirban Lahiri, Shubhankar Sharma and Aditi Ashok, who narrowly missed a medal at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.

 

• Terms of other sports frequently asked:
◦ Archery — bull's eye, quiver, nock, fletching
◦ Polo — chukker, mallet, bunker
◦ Bowling — strike, spare, pin, gutter
◦ Handball — penalty line, free throw line

 

NOTE

 

• Archery (Option 2): Uses terms such as bull's eye, quiver and nock.

 

• Polo (Option 3): Uses chukker for a period of play, and mallet for the stick.

 

• Bowling (Option 4): Uses strike, spare and pin.

question: Which Indian city was the first to be included in the UNESCO World Heritage City list?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ahmedabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ahmedabad in Gujarat became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City in July 2017, when the Historic City of Ahmedabad was inscribed on the World Heritage List. (अहमदाबाद — भारत का पहला विश्व धरोहर शहर)

 

• The city was founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah I on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati. The inscription recognises its rich architectural heritage — the Bhadra citadel, the Jama Masjid, the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque with its celebrated stone tracery, the Teen Darwaza, the pols (traditional residential clusters) and the Sabarmati Ashram.

 

• Jaipur, the walled city of Rajasthan, became India's second World Heritage City in 2019.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• India has a large number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, comprising cultural, natural and mixed properties. The first Indian sites, inscribed in 1983, were the Agra Fort, the Taj Mahal, the Ajanta Caves and the Ellora Caves.

 

• Natural sites in India include Kaziranga, Keoladeo, Manas, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers and the Western Ghats. Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim is India's only mixed site.

 

• UNESCO — the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization — was founded in 1945 and has its headquarters at Paris, France. The World Heritage Convention was adopted in 1972.

 

NOTE

 

• Hyderabad (Option 1): Designated a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2019, which is a different distinction altogether.

 

• Jaipur (Option 2): Inscribed in 2019, making it India's second World Heritage City.

 

• Varanasi (Option 3): One of the oldest living cities in the world, but not on the World Heritage City list.

question: The Charminar at Hyderabad was built by which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Charminar was built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda, who also founded the city of Hyderabad. (चारमीनार — मुहम्मद कुली कुतुब शाह, 1591)

 

• It is said to have been built to commemorate the end of a plague in the city, or alternatively to mark the founding of the new capital. Its name means "four minarets" — it has four graceful minarets, each 56 metres high, rising from a square structure with four arches.

 

• It is built of granite, limestone, mortar and pulverised marble, and the Makkah Masjid stands close by. The monument is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India.

 

• Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was also a poet, and is regarded as the first poet of the Urdu (Dakhini) language to compile a *diwan*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Qutb Shahi dynasty ruled Golconda from 1518 to 1687, when it was annexed by Aurangzeb. It was one of the five Deccan Sultanates that emerged from the break-up of the Bahmani kingdom — the others being the Adil Shahis of Bijapur, the Nizam Shahis of Ahmadnagar, the Imad Shahis of Berar and the Barid Shahis of Bidar.

 

• The combined forces of the Deccan Sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara Empire at the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

 

• The Golconda Fort, famous for its acoustics and once the centre of the diamond trade, and the Qutb Shahi tombs are the other major monuments of the dynasty.

 

NOTE

 

• Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (Option 1): The fourth ruler, the father of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, under whom Golconda prospered.

 

• Quli Qutb Mulk (Option 2): The founder of the Qutb Shahi dynasty in 1518, but not the builder of the Charminar.

 

• Abdullah Qutb Shah (Option 3): The seventh ruler of the dynasty, in whose reign Mughal pressure on Golconda increased.

question: The International Labour Organization (ILO) was established in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1919.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The International Labour Organization (ILO) was established in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, as an agency of the League of Nations, at the end of the First World War. (अंतर्राष्ट्रीय श्रम संगठन — 1919)

 

• In 1946 it became the first specialised agency of the United Nations. Its headquarters is at Geneva, Switzerland, and it was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969, on its fiftieth anniversary.

 

• The ILO is unique among UN bodies for its tripartite structure, in which governments, employers and workers are all represented — in the ratio of 2:1:1.

 

• Its three principal organs are the International Labour Conference (which meets annually in June at Geneva), the Governing Body (its executive council) and the International Labour Office (its permanent secretariat).

 

• India is a founding member of the ILO and has been a permanent member of its Governing Body since 1922.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Years of establishment of major international organisations, frequently asked together:
◦ League of Nations — 1920 (dissolved 1946)
◦ United Nations — 24 October 1945, headquarters New York
◦ UNESCO — 1945, Paris
◦ FAO — 1945, Rome
◦ UNICEF — 1946, New York
◦ WHO — 7 April 1948, Geneva
◦ IMF and World Bank — 1944 (Bretton Woods Conference), Washington D.C.
◦ WTO — 1 January 1995, Geneva, replacing the GATT

 

NOTE

 

• 1945 (Option 2): The year the United Nations itself was founded, and also UNESCO and the FAO.

 

• 1946 (Option 3): The year the ILO became a specialised agency of the UN, not the year of its establishment.

 

• 1948 (Option 4): The year the World Health Organization was established.

question: The Arjuna Award, given for outstanding performance in sports, was instituted in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1961.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Arjuna Award was instituted in 1961 by the Government of India to recognise outstanding performance in sports over a period of four years, along with qualities of leadership, sportsmanship and discipline. (अर्जुन पुरस्कार — 1961)

 

• The award consists of a bronze statuette of Arjuna, a scroll of honour and a cash prize.

 

• The other national sports awards and the years of their institution:
◦ Dronacharya Award — 1985, for outstanding coaches
◦ Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award — 1991-92, the highest sporting honour in India; formerly the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna, renamed in 2021. Its first recipient was Viswanathan Anand.
◦ Dhyan Chand Award — 2002, for lifetime achievement in sports
◦ Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puraskar — 2009, for corporate and other entities that promote sport
◦ Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy — for the best performing university in inter-university tournaments

 

• The awards are conferred by the President of India, usually on 29 August, which is National Sports Day, the birth anniversary of Major Dhyan Chand.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's civilian awards, for comparison, were instituted in 1954 — the Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri.

 

• The Khelo India programme was launched in 2018 to develop grassroots sport, and the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) supports elite athletes.

 

NOTE

 

• 1951 (Option 1): The year of the first Asian Games, held at New Delhi, but not of the Arjuna Award.

 

• 1985 (Option 3): The year the Dronacharya Award for coaches was instituted.

 

• 1991 (Option 4): The year the Khel Ratna, India's highest sporting award, was instituted.

question: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) has its headquarters in which city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Montreal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) has its headquarters at Montreal, Canada. (वाडा — मॉन्ट्रियल, कनाडा)

 

• It was established on 10 November 1999 at Lausanne, Switzerland, on the initiative of the International Olympic Committee, following the First World Conference on Doping in Sport held earlier that year. Its headquarters was later moved to Montreal.

 

• WADA publishes the World Anti-Doping Code, which harmonises anti-doping rules across sports and countries, and issues the annual Prohibited List of substances and methods.

 

• India's national anti-doping body is the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA), established in 2005, with the National Dope Testing Laboratory (NDTL) at New Delhi. The National Anti-Doping Act was passed in 2022.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Headquarters of major sports bodies, frequently asked together:
◦ International Olympic Committee (IOC) — Lausanne, Switzerland; founded 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin
◦ FIFA (football) — Zurich, Switzerland
◦ ICC (cricket) — Dubai, UAE
◦ FIH (hockey) — Lausanne, Switzerland
◦ BWF (badminton) — Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
◦ World Athletics — Monaco
◦ FIDE (chess) — Lausanne, Switzerland

 

NOTE

 

• Lausanne (Option 2): The city where WADA was founded in 1999 and the seat of the IOC, but not its present headquarters.

 

• Geneva (Option 3): Headquarters of the WHO, ILO, WTO and the Red Cross.

 

• Paris (Option 4): Headquarters of UNESCO and the OECD.

question: The Tarapur Atomic Power Station, India's first nuclear power plant, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS), India's first nuclear power plant, is located at Tarapur in the Palghar district of Maharashtra. It began commercial operation in 1969. (तारापुर परमाणु ऊर्जा संयंत्र — महाराष्ट्र)

 

• Its first two units were Boiling Water Reactors (BWRs) built with American assistance under an agreement of 1963. Two later units use Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs), the design on which India's indigenous programme is based.

 

• Nuclear power plants in India and their states:
◦ Tarapur — Maharashtra
◦ Rawatbhata (Rajasthan Atomic Power Station) — Rajasthan
◦ Kalpakkam (Madras Atomic Power Station) — Tamil Nadu
◦ Narora — Uttar Pradesh
◦ Kakrapar — Gujarat
◦ Kaiga — Karnataka
◦ Kudankulam — Tamil Nadu, built with Russian assistance and the largest in India

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nuclear power in India is managed by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), under the Department of Atomic Energy. The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948 and the Department of Atomic Energy in 1954, both under Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha, who is called the Father of the Indian Nuclear Programme.

 

• India's three-stage nuclear programme, devised by Dr. Bhabha, moves from PHWRs using natural uranium, to Fast Breeder Reactors using plutonium, and finally to reactors using India's vast reserves of thorium, found chiefly in the monazite sands of Kerala.

 

• India's first nuclear test, Pokhran-I (Smiling Buddha), was conducted on 18 May 1974, and Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) in May 1998.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 2): Site of the Kakrapar Atomic Power Station in the Tapi district.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Site of the Rawatbhata plant near Kota, India's second nuclear power station.

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 4): Site of Kalpakkam and Kudankulam.

question: Who was the first Indian woman to win the Miss World title?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Reita Faria.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Reita Faria became the first Indian woman — and the first Asian woman — to win the Miss World title, in 1966. (रीता फारिया — प्रथम भारतीय मिस वर्ल्ड, 1966)

 

• She was a medical student at the time, and after her reign she declined offers in films and modelling, completed her medical education in London and practised as a doctor. She is remembered as the only Miss World to have qualified as a physician.

 

• Indian winners of the Miss World title: Reita Faria (1966), Aishwarya Rai (1994), Diana Hayden (1997), Yukta Mookhey (1999), Priyanka Chopra (2000) and Manushi Chhillar (2017).

 

• Indian winners of the Miss Universe title: Sushmita Sen (1994), Lara Dutta (2000) and Harnaaz Sandhu (2021).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The year 1994 is memorable in this context because Sushmita Sen won Miss Universe and Aishwarya Rai won Miss World in the same year — a distinction candidates are often asked to separate.

 

• The Miss World pageant was founded in 1951 by Eric Morley in the United Kingdom; Miss Universe was first held in 1952.

 

NOTE

 

• Sushmita Sen (Option 2): Winner of Miss Universe in 1994, not Miss World.

 

• Aishwarya Rai (Option 3): Winner of Miss World in 1994, but the second Indian to do so, not the first.

 

• Diana Hayden (Option 4): Winner of Miss World in 1997.
